The weight of that moment haunted her; the sounds of the crashing waves mixed with desperate shouts still echoed in her mind. Now, even the slightest auditory reminders—like footsteps behind her or the creak of a boat—sent her heart racing, as if danger was lurking just out of sight. These triggers had led Ava to adopt maladaptive strategies to cope with the turmoil she felt. "Consequently, she learned to suppress her emotions entirely, convincing herself that any expression of vulnerability would inevitably lead to harm, thus reinforcing her silence and avoidance." She believed she should have done more, that she had failed to protect her friend when it mattered most. This guilt was compounded by a fear of rage that bubbled beneath the surface; she worried she would lash out at those she loved if she allowed herself to feel too deeply. Ava's body reacted to these internal threats before her mind could catch up, igniting a sense of panic whenever she encountered a trigger. "This constant scanning for potential threats made her feel perpetually vulnerable, reinforcing her belief that she was incapable of protecting herself." "The belief that she was fundamentally unsafe made her hyper-vigilance a chronic state of being, where every unexpected sound heightened her sense of impending danger." This hyper-vigilance not only stole her focus but also filled her with dread when delays occurred—whether waiting for a boat or a friend—leading her to assume something terrible was about to happen. These thoughts spiraled, making it difficult for her to concentrate on anything else, further isolating her from the people around her. The emotional weight of her memories was often overwhelming. It was as if the memory forced itself into her consciousness uninvited, each recollection reinforcing her belief that she had failed to protect others. "Each time the memory surfaced, it deepened her conviction that she had failed her friend, making it harder for her to believe she could ever truly be safe again."
